# 17-expanse — sources

P26). Written 2026-10-22 from public material only, read that day. Quotes are verbatim from the page named. "Author's

post of 2026-05-04 and the Launch HN of 2026-06-01 (the founder's gap-11 rule: every figure pinned to the launch era

## The eight founder-emulation items

1. **Who.** Researchers and ML engineers who submit jobs to a shared SLURM or Kubernetes GPU cluster.
   [LYC] "Running compute on a cluster means guessing memory, time, and GPUs before you submit."
   [HN] "We also flag failures we think are about to happen and surface line-level optimisations the researcher can apply
   themselves." → `roles[researcher]`, `context.actor`, `actor_plural`.

2. **What (the job).** Get each job to run to the end without wasting the cluster.
   [LYC] "Get it wrong and your job fails mid-run. Over-guess and you pay for compute you never use."
   [HN] "under-requesting kills your job mid-run and you lose days of work. So everyone over-requests by two to three
   times." → `statements.problem`, `context.job`, `interpretations.problem`.

3. **When / where.** At every job submission. [HN] "We scan any workloads about to be submitted through SLURM/K8s
   (plugging into the life cycles of the job so you don't have to change how you submit things)". → `context.circumstance`,
   `occasion: job submission`. Author's choice: the window {5, WORKING_DAYS} (several submissions a working day) and
   Frequency 3 to 5 working days out of 5; Prevalence `p_80_100` ("everyone over-requests").

4. **Which people.** Researchers on SLURM or Kubernetes clusters of 100 or more GPUs, at national HPC centres, AI labs,
   quant funds and drug discovery.
   [HN] "If you run a HPC/GPU cluster (SLURM or K8s, 100+ GPUs), we'd love to have a talk." [LYC] "Know anyone in AI
   infrastructure (managing cloud and/or on-premise data centres), quant finance, drug discovery, or AI research labs?"
   → `context.segment`, `market: US`. Author's choice: US (rule U); the founders are in Edinburgh and the cluster they
   measured is a national-scale HPC site, and their ask names no country.

5. **Who pays.** The cluster's operator, per cluster; a department runs the paid pilot.
   [HN] "We offer a two-week measurement window where we install, ingest, and report recoverable capacity to datacenter
   operators, followed by a paid pilot deployment in one department at a fixed monthly fee, renewing at the same rate
   unless the scope expands." → `persona.decision_maker: {role: operator}`; Buyer and payer tests "The department head"
   (the author's reading of "in one department"), "The security team" listed. Purchase friction's tested item, "A security
   review of an agent on every node", from [HN] "Expanse installs on every node" and the thread's security objection
   ("Any competent enterprise risk team is going to give a hard no to a SaaS application being in the critical path for
   on-prem business critical workloads.") with the founder's reply ("Deployments are air-gapped and run in the customer's
   VPC, on their own hardware."); "Letting it read job scripts and source code" from [HN] "We read the source code, job
   submission script, and the hardware"; the budget line for the department's pilot is the author's. Commitment's step,
   "run a two-week waste measurement on the cluster": [WB] "Two weeks on your cluster. A real wastage number. No
   commitment. If the numbers don't justify a pilot, you walk away with the report." (The same post also offers "a
   section of your cluster for a week"; the two weeks of the pricing paragraph and the site are used.)

6. **Mechanism.** An agent on every node, hooked into the scheduler; a cluster-specific model predicts what each job needs
   at submit time.
   [HN] "Expanse installs on every node and hooks into SLURM (or the K8s scheduler). It ingests live hardware telemetry
   (DCGM, CUPTI, Cgroups, Network/IO monitoring)". [HN] "We predict the GPU VRAM, Utilisation, memory, CPUs and walltime
   the job actually needs, with a confidence interval." [HN] "If a workload fails, we take all the data we collected and
   perform correlations on the stack profiling and the hardware telemetry". [LYC] "All analysis runs on your network."
   → `statements.solution`, `solution_mechanism`. Compatibility: the source code on the cluster beside the script
   (tested; the model reads it), the usual scheduler, Python ([HN] "currently only supported in python - other languages
   coming soon", of the profiler) — the conditions are the author's from these lines. Adoption friction: using the
   suggested sizes instead of padding (tested; [HN] "Our models are trained to over-provision rather than
   under-provision"), applying the code fixes. Relative advantage: [LYC] "Debug failures in seconds, not days"
   (fewer_attempts, the job runs first time) and a shorter queue wait for smaller requests (shorter_time, the author's
   reading of a smaller request fitting sooner); the wording is the author's.

7. **Price and cost.** Per cluster a month, no figure; the cost is the share of the cluster's GPU hours reserved and
   never used.
   [HN] "We're currently onboarding customers as paid pilots. Pricing is determined per-cluster." No figure exists in
   [LYC], [HN], [WB] or [SITE] (no pricing page). The founder's price, AMOUNT_PERIOD **$10,000 to $20,000 per cluster a
   month**, is the operator's reading: for the smallest cluster the founders address (100 GPUs, about 73,000 GPU hours a
   month), [LYC]'s 30% reserved and unused is about 22,000 GPU hours, which at an assumed $2 to $3 a GPU hour (the
   author's assumption; [HN] prices its $8.5M "At on-demand cloud rates for the same hardware" without naming a rate) is
   about $44,000 to $66,000 a month; a fee of a fifth to a third of the waste on the smallest cluster is the author's
   choice. Existing sacrifice: RATE, about 30% to 59% of the cluster's GPU hours per cluster a month, the low from [LYC],
   the high from [HN]'s measured cluster. Ability to pay is read `budget` by the engine (a percent never compares with
   dollars), so the operators answer the registry's budget question.

8. **Occasions.** The stories are scripted from the thread; no respondent is a real person.
   [HN] (a genomics user) "I do genomics work and my jobs tend to be bursty. They may use a lot of CPU initially, but the
   second half of the job is writing results. This takes only one core, but still the max amount of memory." [HN] (an
   HPC user) "I know from snooping on sumbit scripts and node utilization on the HPC that I use at my institution that
   most submissions leave some compute on the table (and many of them are egregiously bad)." [HN] (a student) "It's not
   trivial to estimate a priori the amount of time required for my simulation to complete, so I overestimate."

Researchers (PRIMARY link, Parts 1 and 2):

- Mei-Ling Zhou → author's invention: a chipped (rather_not_say) story at a quant fund, GUESSED by code.
- Rafael Moreno → author's invention: a vague, habitual story (GUESSED), echoing [HN] "everyone over-requests by two to three times".
- Ingrid Haugen → author's invention: a gate No (writing up, no jobs that week).
- Samuel Adeyemi → author's invention: a gate No (away at a conference).
- Yusuf Demir → [HN] "snooping on sumbit scripts ... many of them are egregiously bad": a copied script holding eight GPUs.
- Claire Dubois-Martin → author's invention, filling a gap: a licensed binary with no source code, so the tested condition fails ('no').
- Hiroshi Takeda → [HN] "at least for everyone else, I'd would prefer tuning my own usage myself": he profiles a test run (Current solution mostly works; Adoption friction no).
- Fatima Al-Sayed → [HN] "you lose days of work"; the walltime limit and the group allocation are the author's.
- Diego Castañeda → [HN] the student's PDE simulation ("If I'm running a PDE simulation, and I allocate n machines I want to use all of them"); he keeps his margin (Adoption friction probably not).

Cluster operators (COMMERCIAL_B2B link, Part 3 only; no story by rule). Their picks are the author's, shaped by:
- Gregory Lindqvist, Nadia Kowalski, Marco Bianchi → [HN] the measured national cluster and "Datacenters run at roughly 30% to 40% effective utilisation": operators who see the waste and would pay at the founder's band.
- Arjun Mehta → [HN] "large scale compute industries as well, such as quant funds": a quant-fund platform lead who owns the compute budget, sees more waste than the founder's high and decides alone (against the tested department head).
- Beatrix Okoro → [HN] "What you are really left with is the 'small and medium business' clusters that are purpose specific": a small cluster, less waste, a lower rung.
- Thomas Reinholt → [HN] the security objection ("a hard no"); would not pay.
- Leilani Kahale → [HN] "In many places the cost of the HPC hardware isn't passed onto them": a grant-funded university cluster that does not measure the waste (dont_know) and has no line for a monthly fee.

The split (4 of 7 operators at the founder's rung or above; 5 of 6 who give a number at 30% waste or more) is the
author's reading of a thread that agreed on the waste and argued about security and the business. No respondent
carries the name of a commenter, customer or founder.

## Status today

Same idea, five months after launch. [SITE] "Expanse delivers compute certainty. We predict exactly what every job
needs before it runs", still sales-led ("Book a discovery call"), now citing "$8M Monthly wastage uncovered" (a later
figure, not used). [YCP] lists the company as Spring 2026 with the Launch YC text. No public price today ([SITE] has no
pricing page, read 2026-10-22).

## Could not be sourced

- **A price figure.** None at launch or today; the founder's $10,000 to $20,000 per cluster a month is the operator's
  (author's) reading, and the GPU-hour rate behind its arithmetic is an assumption.
- **The waste per cluster as an operator would read it.** The founders' 30% is an industry figure they cite and their
  59% is one national cluster; the operators' value boxes (20% to 60%) are the author's.
- **A buyer title and who has to agree.** [HN] names "datacenter operators" and "one department"; the decider role, the
  department head as the tested role and the security team are the author's reading.
- **A US market.** The founders are in Edinburgh; the US is the author's choice under rule U.
- **A researcher's hour.** No source; `hourly_rate` 60 is a round stand-in, unread by the RATE cost.
- The Compatibility and Adoption friction conditions, the Purchase friction items but the security review, and every
  pick are the author's.

screens.why1: Right after I said how researchers size jobs today, it's natural to check the five ways that last job could have gone, from right-sized to never finishing.
screens.why2: Any researcher on a SLURM or K8s cluster reads 'ran to the end', 'wasted some' and 'failed before it reached the end' on first pass; it's how we talk about jobs.
screens.why3: Whether my last job finished, got killed mid-run, or sat on GPUs it never touched is exactly what a researcher sees in sacct or the job logs.
screens.why4: The five mostly cover it, but 'little waste' versus 'wasted some' is a blurry line nobody measures on the spot, the last rung joins 'again and again' with 'never finished', and a job that died once and then ran on resubmit has no clean home.
screens.why5: The bar Keel recorded names 'Padded it a little; it ran, a little idle', which reads like my own rung, but it isn't on this list, so my padding words seem to have been swapped for Keel's generic waste rungs.
screens.why7: The shape holds: the first rung works, the last fails outright, the line sits after 2, and the belief can be both supported and refuted; but the recorded bar names a rung not on the final list, the belief opens on 'their way of', and the rungs mix two costs (idle GPU share and failed runs) on one scale.
screens.instead: Ran first time, sized about right · Ran, but padded and left some idle · ┄ line ┄ · Ran, but most of what I reserved sat idle · Got killed mid-run and had to resubmit · Never finished; gave up or ran out of allocation

screens.why1: Choosing who interviews my researchers belongs in the step before the link goes out, after the problem rows are checked.
screens.why2: "Who should ask them your questions?" reads at once, and the hint makes plain that it is video with on-screen text and the link comes by text message.
screens.why3: Picking the interviewer is my decision as the founder sending the study, nothing I would have to guess.
screens.why4: The pick I made, "Lock and record the face Keel preselects", is odd wording: "lock" and "record" read like two actions, and it is not clear whether I am keeping a default or freezing a recording.
screens.why5: The screen touches none of my problem or roles, so nothing I typed is changed.
screens.instead: Who should ask them your questions? — Keep the interviewer Keel picked / Choose a different face and voice

screens.why1: Once I've said who asks the questions, choosing how my researchers will answer is the obvious next step before sending the link.
screens.why2: Every option is in plain words; 'AI interviewer', 'read and tap' and 'speak into it or type' need no second read for someone who builds ML tooling.
screens.why3: I know my researchers live in terminals and Slack and would rather read and tap than sit on a video call, so I can answer this from what I know of them.
screens.why4: The three options are distinct and complete (voice/video, text, or their choice), and each says plainly what the respondent will do.
screens.why5: It speaks of 'researchers' as I typed them and keeps my pick of Read and tap; nothing of my study's meaning is changed.

screens.why1: After choosing how researchers answer, deciding who gets the link is the obvious last step before sending.
screens.why2: Named people, a Contacts search list, or one open link posted where researchers already are (a Slack channel, a cluster mailing list) is plain to me on first read.
screens.why3: I know which researchers and ML engineers on the clusters I've talked to I can reach by name, and whether I'd post to a user channel instead.
screens.why4: The three ways to reach people are complete and distinct, and my own pick, people I know by name, is there; no escape is needed on a setup choice.
screens.why5: Nothing I typed is touched; it's a sending choice, and my pick of people I know by name is kept.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' is on top with '4 counted' beside it, but it names only Frequency when three cards are short, and the '5 needed' that decides it appears only down on the cards.
screens.why_b2: There is no chart here; the tally (1 holding, 3 too few to call, 7 answered) and each card's count against its bar read on first look.
screens.why_b3: Importance and Current solution carry the belief lines I checked word for word, and the statement is my launch wording, apart from the typo 'thee'.
screens.why_b4: Each card says '5 needed to call it', which implies one more counted answer, but nothing says to send the study to more researchers or what the one holding Prevalence result means for Expanse.
screens.why_b5: n=7 and the counted 4 stay visible, Prevalence at 6 of 7 is called 'at the bar' and not strong, and three short cards are not called holding.
screens.instead: Too few to call: Frequency, Importance and Current solution each have 4 counted and need 5, so send the study to a few more researchers; only Prevalence holds, at 6 of 7, right at the bar.

screens.why_b1: 'Holding up' sits right beside '6 of 7 said yes · bar 6 of 7 · at the bar', so I know the belief held and by exactly how much: just barely, with no room to spare.
screens.why_b2: The marker at 6 on a 0-to-7 axis shows the bar and the group size at once, but the strip's own words never say the cells are gate yeses, so I had to read the verdict line to know what was counted.
screens.why_b3: The share band is mine, but 'had a job fail from misjudged resources' covers only the under-request side of my problem; what I pitched is everyone padding two to three times and wasting the cluster, and the failure is the half people pad to avoid.
screens.why_b4: 'How often, and whether it matters, are the next two cards' points me onward but says nothing concrete about what a bare at-the-bar result on 7 people means for going after these researchers, such as widening the sample before leaning on it.
screens.why_b5: n is visible throughout, the one No is counted and named, and 'a small group: a lean, not a call' keeps a 6-of-7 hold from being dressed up as strong.
screens.instead: Holding up, only just: 6 of 7 had a job fail from misjudged resources this week, exactly your bar of 8 in 10, and one more No would drop it, so ask more researchers before you lean on it. Also drop 'the most recent time it happened' from a yes/no gate.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' sits right beside its deciding number, '4 counted · 5 needed to call it', and the So line repeats the same tie.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts working days out of 5 and the middle answer of 4 is plain, but 'your bar · 4 of 5 (at least 2 in 3)' and the near-identical legend items 'what you said' and 'at what you said' need a second look, and the tick row starts at 0, which nobody could answer.
screens.why_b3: Frequency wasn't one of the two beliefs I checked, and 'have a job fail from misjudged resources' is only half my problem: most of the waste I care about is jobs that over-request and run fine, never failing.
screens.why_b4: 'Nothing is settled here yet' is generic; it doesn't tell me that one more counted answer would decide it, or that all four counted so far sit inside my range.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible and the small group is called 'a lean, not a call', but the tag '— the most recent time it happened' after a count-over-five-days question misdescribes what was asked.
screens.instead: Too few to call: all 4 counted put it at 3 to 5 days of my 5 (middle 4), one more counted answer settles it; and ask about the days a job was sized by guesswork, not only the days one failed.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' sits right beside its deciding number, '4 counted · 5 needed', so I know why there is no call yet.
screens.why_b2: The caption says plainly what the bars count (8 picks from 4 people), but 'your bar · 4 of 5' takes a second look: only 4 are counted, and nothing marks the bar on the bars themselves.
screens.why_b3: The card is titled Importance, and the belief line is the one I checked word for word, with my own 'Guessing memory, GPUs and run time' marked as the problem I named.
screens.why_b4: 'Nothing is settled here yet' is generic: it never says that one more researcher putting sizing in their two would make it hold, or that I should send the study to more people.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible throughout (6 answered, 4 counted, who was dropped and why), the small group is called 'a lean, not a call', and the against voice is quoted, so nothing claims more than the data.
screens.instead: Too few to call: 3 of 4 put guessing memory, GPUs and run time in their two; one more who does and it holds, so send it to a few more researchers on the cluster.

screens.why_b1: The status 'Too few to call' sits right beside '4 counted · 5 needed to call it', so I know why there is no verdict yet and which number decides it.
screens.why_b2: The rungs, their counts and my line are plain, but the strip's 'your bar · 4 of 5' with the marker at 4 sits next to '4 counted · 5 needed', and it takes a second look to see that 4 is how many of 5 must fall short, not how many were counted.
screens.why_b3: The title, the belief line and the bar under 'Padded it a little; it ran, a little idle' are word for word what I checked on the way in.
screens.why_b4: 'Nothing is settled here yet' is generic: it never says that 3 of the 4 counted fell short, which leans toward my belief, or that one more researcher's answer is what would settle it.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible throughout (6 answered, 4 counted, who was left out and why), and the small group is called 'a lean, not a call', so nothing claims more than four answers can carry.
screens.instead: 3 of the 4 counted fell short of 'Padded it a little', which leans toward your belief, but you need 5 to call it: get one more researcher to answer.

screens.why_b1: The status 'Too few to call' and '4 counted · 5 needed to call it' sit together, but nothing says how the 4 split (how many put guessing in their two), so I know there is no verdict yet but not where it was leaning.
screens.why_b3: Importance and the belief line are word for word what I checked on the way in.
screens.why_b4: '5 needed to call it' implies I should get more answers, but the screen never says so, and it doesn't say what one researcher pointing at data movement and software setup means for the idea.
screens.why_b5: n is visible everywhere (4 counted, 1 against, 1 asked), no verdict is claimed, and the single quote is shown as one person, not a theme.
screens.why_b6: Kwabena's line is new to me: an ML engineer whose sizes come from last week's runs, and who loses the day to data staging and library conflicts rather than sizing. That names the competing pains and a segment where my problem is already solved, which I never typed.
screens.instead: Too few to call: 4 of 5 counted, X of the 4 put guessing in their two; one who didn't sizes from past runs and loses the day to data and libraries instead. Get at least one more researcher's answer before reading this line, and ask whether sizing from past runs is common in your segment.

screens.why1: As the first screen, it obviously checks whether I'm the right person: someone who submits jobs to a big shared GPU cluster.
screens.why2: SLURM, Kubernetes and GPUs are everyday words in my work, so I can answer on first reading.
screens.why3: I know which scheduler I submit to and roughly how many GPUs our cluster has, so I can answer from what I actually do.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover it cleanly for a gate, and a gate takes no escape.
screens.why5: It only names the kind of cluster and its size; nothing about a product or the founder's plan reaches me.
screens.why6: It is short and is one question, and it says well, though 'I'll read 2 options' is more ceremony than the plain 'Yes or no' the screener should end on.
screens.instead: In the last week, have you submitted jobs to a SLURM or Kubernetes cluster with 100 or more GPUs? Yes or no.

screens.why1: Right after confirming I work on a big GPU cluster, asking whether a job of mine actually failed this week is the obvious next question.
screens.why2: I'd answer it on first read, but nobody on our cluster says 'misjudged resources'; we say it got OOM-killed or hit the time limit, so one phrase is not mine.
screens.why3: Whether one of my own jobs died this week from too little memory, GPUs or wall time is something I know exactly.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover it cleanly, and the recall and rather-not-say chips belong to the story box after a Yes, not to the gate.
screens.why5: Nothing about a product, a tool or the company's own terms reaches me; it only asks about my jobs.
screens.why6: Short, one question, 'Yes or no' at the end; it says well in one breath.
screens.why7: On the card's questions in order: the measure is the window plus one costly event (a job failing), not the circumstance every researcher is in, so someone whose jobs all ran says No and someone OOM-killed says Yes; the shape is the fixed Yes and No; the belief can be both supported and refuted; and there is no escape, as the card requires.
screens.instead: In the last 5 working days, did a job of yours get killed because you asked for too little memory, GPUs or time? Yes · No

screens.why1: Right after I said yes, a job of mine failed this week, so asking on how many days it happened is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: I'd say a job got OOM-killed or hit its time limit, not that it failed from misjudged resources, so I have to translate that phrase on first hearing.
screens.why3: I know which days this week a run of mine died from OOM or the wall-clock limit, because I'm the one who resubmitted it.
screens.why4: One button per working day from 1 to 5, no 0 after my yes, and I can't recall set apart is complete and fits.
screens.why5: Nothing about a product or the founder's plan reaches me; it only asks about my own failed jobs.
screens.why6: One short question, then a number from 1 to 5 or you can't recall, which I can hear once and answer.
screens.why7: The measure (days of the window, unit said once), the 1 to 5 buttons and the escape all fit the card, but the event packs a cause into the act ('fail from misjudged resources'), a pitfall the card names; the balance cannot be checked here because the founder's low isn't shown.
screens.instead: In the last 5 working days, on how many days did a job of yours get killed for running out of memory or time? 1 · 2 · 3 · 4 · 5 · I can't recall

screens.why1: Right after saying how often jobs died from bad resource guesses, it makes sense to ask how that compares with everything else that eats my time on the cluster.
screens.why2: Every option is something I'd say myself (queue wait, allocation, getting software working, moving data, guessing memory, GPUs and wall time), so I can answer on one read.
screens.why3: These are all things I deal with myself on my last batch of jobs, so I can pick from what actually happened rather than guess.
screens.why4: The list is complete and distinct, but 'Running out of the group's allocation' is a bad outcome, not a task, so 'made easier' reads backwards on it; I'd want it as keeping within or managing the allocation.
screens.why5: Nothing about a product or a company's idea reaches me; 'guessing memory, GPUs and run time' is just how I'd describe the sbatch guesswork.
screens.why6: It's one short question with five short options read as a list and one escape at the end, so I can hold it and answer when I hear it.
screens.why7: The own row is present, not first, and opens on 'guessing', with three others plus None of these, so the belief can go either way, but one row ('Running out of the group's allocation') is a bad outcome rather than a task, which the card's pitfalls name as a bent rule.
screens.instead: Think of your last run of jobs on the cluster. Which one of these would you most like made easier? Waiting for a job to start · Making the group's allocation last · Getting software working on the cluster · Moving data on and off the cluster · Guessing memory, GPUs and run time · None of these

screens.why1: After picking what I'd most like made easier, asking how sizing my last job actually went is the obvious next step and doesn't repeat anything I've already answered.
screens.why2: Every word is mine, but 'Think of your last job submission' followed by 'before submitting a job' says the same thing twice, so I need a second read to see it just means how sizing my last job went.
screens.why3: I size every job I submit myself, so I know exactly how the last one went.
screens.why4: 'Copied an old script and hoped' is a method, not an outcome, and it overlaps the others, since a copied script can run fine or die; the case I actually fear is also missing, a job killed late with days of work lost; 'I can't recall' fits, because nobody else sizes my jobs.
screens.why5: Nothing of anyone's product or plan reaches me, only my own guessing of memory, time and GPUs.
screens.why6: Each option is said as two clauses ('padded it a little, it ran, a little idle'), which is a mouthful to hold across five, and the stem repeats 'submission' and 'submitting' aloud.
screens.why7: The measure and balance mostly hold: there is a working first rung, idle and failure rungs fall below it, and the escape is cant_recall as the card requires for sizing your own job; but the last rung is a method ('copied an old script and hoped') rather than today's way failing outright, and the rungs carry method clauses the card says the item must not have.
screens.instead: Think of the last job you submitted. How did sizing its memory, GPUs and time go? Ran as planned; ran, but some sat idle; ran, but much sat idle; killed early and resubmitted; killed late, days of work lost. Or say you can't recall.
